About me

I'm Namitha, a product designer from Bengaluru who believes good design starts with listening, not with a screen. I'd rather understand a problem than decorate it, and I won't dress up a guess as a finding. I design for the person doing the work, keep the business in the room, and want everything I make to be honest, useful and easy to trust.

Final-year Interaction Design, PES University · Bengaluru · Graduating 2027

How a project goes

Go to the place.

Stand where the work actually happens, before anything else.

Field research

Watch the work.

How people do it today, what slows them down and what they quietly work around.

User research

Map the whole system.

Every person, step and handover, drawn out as journeys and service blueprints.

Service design

Find what the business needs.

The vision, the goals and the numbers that would show it's working.

Product strategy

Then I open Figma.

Flows, screens and prototypes, built from what I saw out there.

Product and UX design

Take it back outside.

Check it where it will be used, with the people who will use it.

Testing · Spatial and AR

The work is on the right page

Measure the roof. Plan the panels.

AR rooftop survey

Easy to measure, until the roof isn't a rectangle

Over 50 lakh Indian homes had rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar by July 2026. Every one began with a site survey: someone on a terrace with a measuring tape, a phone camera and the electricity bill. Tanks, stair rooms and parapets turn a simple job into a page of numbers.

If the survey misses it, the design team calls back.

So I went up on the roof

Two site visits in Bengaluru, and conversations with two solar company founders and a manager. The rest sounded like this:

# rooftop-survey5 people · paraphrased
01

Measuring the roof and drawing the layout is the slow, manual part.

Founder
02

How long does one house take?

Me
03

It depends on the house. Every roof is different.

Manager
04

If a size is missing or a photo is unclear, the design team has to call back.

Founder
05

Customers can't picture the panels from a 2D drawing.

Founder

Tools already exist

Existing tools are

a measuring tapea drawing appArka360Aurora SolarLiDAR scan apps

They measure from a desk or from a photo taken above. None of them check the roof while you're standing on it.

Who it's for

Three proto-personas from the research. One person uses it; the other two depend on what he captures.

#01Selvan, 31 · Field surveyor

Measures every roof by hand, then gets the call back anyway.

Puts up withTape lengths, scattered photos and the owner's guess at the house size.
the roof
#02Saanvi, 29 · Design engineer

Draws the layout for a roof she has never stood on.

Puts up withMissing dimensions, unclear photos and tanks with no height.
#03Anand, 42 · Homeowner

Has to approve panels he can only see on a 2D drawing.

Puts up withQuestions about the tank, the walkway and the shade.

Why on the roof

The roof is the only place where every number can be checked. Every surveyor already carries a phone, and AR can measure without LiDAR. The roof door gives one fixed point to measure everything from.

Where panels can't go

A 55.2 m² terrace, three rules. Try the three states.

45.7m² usable
7panels

A 0.30 m walkway all round leaves 45.7 m² usable, room for 7 panels.

Inside the app

Each corner gets its own anchor, every height is measured by aiming at it, and the plan turns to face the way you are standing.

Measure the roof. Plan the panels.

  • Home
  • Tap the corners
  • Tape check
  • Panel layout
  • Panel plan

How it flows

Seven steps, one walk round the roof.

01 / 04

Arrive

Mark the door

Every point is measured from the roof entry.

Trace

Walk the edge

Tap each corner where the floor meets the parapet.

Check

Tape one edge

If AR and tape differ by more than 10 cm, place the corners again.

Show

Plan it on the roof

Type the bill, see the panels on the real roof, and save the plan for the design team.

Try the flow

Drag the slider or tap the screen.

EntryCornersTapePanelsPlan

Before the visit, too

Map Check traces the same roof on satellite imagery at the desk, with the same panel and shade rules. Heights still have to be typed in, so it gives a first look, not a measurement.

Reflections

  1. The tape stayed.I set out to replace the measuring tape. Drift on plain terraces made it a check instead: one taped edge, within ±10 cm.
  2. Corners go at the foot of the wall.Early taps landed on furniture and drifted as I walked. One anchor per corner fixed both.
  3. Working is not validated.It runs on a real terrace. Whether it saves field staff time is the next test, with them.
Case study · On the coworking floor

Nexus · case study

Workspace, made social.

A social layer for Bengaluru coworking spaces: an app, plus a status light on every desk.

A coworking floor is full of people.

And nobody talks.

Is she free to talk? Don't want to interrupt…

It breaks at three moments.

BeforeArriving blind DuringA wall of silence AfterLost connections
No way to know who will be there, or whether the space suits the day's work. No signal of who is open to talk, so headphones stay on. Conversations that almost happened have nowhere to continue.

So I asked members why.

Freelancers People who work there every day How do you meet people here? What stops you? A moment that went well A moment that felt like an interruption

Then I mapped the market. Nobody covered all three moments.

So, a light on every desk.

The system

Discover Arrive Signal Reconnect
See who is likely to be in the space before you go. Check in to a zone when you get there. A desk light shows your status, and a one-tap wave asks to talk without interrupting. A weekly digest helps you pick up with people you nearly met.

Then, the app.

Canopy CoworkDesk C-14 · Focus zoneIn 10 min
Around todayDesign 2Data 4Eng 5
Invisible
Check in

Product strategy

A social intelligence platform for coworking spaces.

Improve professional discovery Reduce networking friction Preserve relationships Strengthen communities

Measured by connections made, status use, repeat visits and monthly retention.

nexusnexusnexusnexusnexusnexusnexus
Workspace, made social.

Headphones on, until you can’t

Coworking sells community, but most days a hot desk is a quiet room full of strangers. Everyone has headphones on, and nobody can tell who’s open to talk.

The right person might be three desks away. Nothing tells you, and there’s no polite way to ask.

So I asked

I talked informally with freelancers and regular members about how they connect and what stops them. It sounded like this:

#the-floorparaphrased
01

I never know who’ll be in before I get there.

02

Everyone has headphones on. I won’t be the one who interrupts.

03

Getting interrupted on a deadline is worse than not talking.

04

I met someone useful once. Never got their name.

05

If I knew they wanted to talk, I’d just say hi.

Tools already exist

Existing tools are

  • booking apps
  • billing tools
  • desk maps
  • LinkedIn
  • event apps
  • not built for the room.

They show desks, invoices and profiles. None of them show who’s open to talk right now.

Who it’s for

Three kinds of people share the floor, and the same problem.

the
floor
#01The solo strategist · Freelancer

Works for herself, with no team, no hallway and no colleague attached.

Puts up withHeadphones on, nobody talks, home with no new names.
#02The satellite employee · Remote

Works for a team elsewhere, with nobody nearby in the same field.

Puts up withA full floor and no idea who’s in their line of work.
Built for themField counts in Around today, the Open list in Here now, and requests that say why you’re reaching out.
#03The domain nomad · Consultant

Picks a space by who’s there, not just by price or Wi-Fi.

Puts up withBooking blind, then finding the wrong crowd.
Built for themThe Explore map, Around today before booking, and “How busy” on space details.

Why a light

Nobody opens an app before saying hi. A light on the desk says it in the room, before anyone has to ask or interrupt.

The signal

One light on every desk, set from your phone. Try the three states.

wave

Lit. Open to a wave or a quick hello.

Inside the app

Five screens from one visit, from finding a space to sitting at the right desk.

Workspace, made social.

  • Home
  • Find a space
  • Who's around
  • Book a zone
  • Pick a desk

How it flows

Before, during and after a visit. Four moments, one line through the day.

01 02 03 04

01Discover

Plan your visit

See how busy a space is and which fields are around, before you leave home.

02Arrive

See who’s open, live

Check in and pick your mode. Only people who chose Open show up.

03Signal

Who’s open today

Your desk light and a one-tap wave do the asking for you.

04Reconnect

Pick up the thread

Save who you met at check-out and find them on your next visit.

Try the flow

One visit, five screens. Tap around inside the phone.

For the host, too

Community managers get a desktop console: who’s in by field, an intro queue, and member privacy they can’t override.

On the wrist, too

Switch modes, answer a wave and confirm check-in without reaching for your phone.

Reflections

  1. Control was the brief.Invisible is the default, and being seen is always your choice.
  2. Ask about moments, not features.One recent real moment told me more than asking what people want.
  3. Build the signal, not the feed.Nexus works by adding a light to the room, not another app to scroll.

IxD · Studio project · 2024 · Redesigned 2026

One vault for every report, shared only on your terms.

MedVault keeps prescriptions, lab reports, X-rays and MRIs in one place. A reusable profile fills hospital forms, but only after the patient approves what goes out, and for how long.

  • Product Design
  • UX Research
  • Health Tech
Role
Research and flows with Meenakshi N. · Redesign and prototype, solo
Year
2024 · 2026
Tools
Figma · Canva · HTML prototype

A concept, not a shipped product. Every patient, doctor and record shown is fictional.

MedVault MedVault MedVault MedVault MedVault MedVault

Every report. One vault.

Paperwork, until you need it

Every hospital visit starts with the same patient form, filled from memory. Old prescriptions and reports sit in drawers, phone galleries and other hospitals' files. 42% of the people we surveyed said the form alone takes them more than 10 minutes.

84% couldn't keep track of the forms they had filled, and 74% didn't have their old prescriptions and receipts.

So we asked

We spoke to patients and doctors. The rest sounded like this:

# opd-waiting-room4 people
Patient

The details form takes me over 15 minutes. At every hospital.

Doctor

Without the old prescription, I'm guessing at drug interactions.

Patient

People who didn't study much can't fill these forms on their own.

Doctor

If the history were already there, I'd decide faster and make fewer mistakes.

Paraphrased from interviews with a software engineer, an Army veteran and two doctors.

Apps that already exist

We studied Practo

Practo Tata 1mg Mfine HealthPlix Amwell Skyscape

Good at bookings, deliveries and doctor-side records. None we studied let the patient decide what a hospital sees, item by item, for one visit.

Who it's for

Four people around one hospital visit.

#01Aditya, 40

Three prescriptions, and no idea where last year's reports went.

Puts up withRefilling the same form at every hospital.
#02Riya, 18

Wants her history handy without retelling it every visit.

Puts up withLost time, stress and errors in forms.
the OPDNow serving01
#03Raj, 72

Never went to school. Hospital forms are written for someone who did.

Puts up withComplex words, required fields, cramped layouts.
#04Dr. Girish

Needs the last prescription before writing the next one.

Puts up withSlow record searches and the risk of drug clashes.

Why consent, not just storage

Storing records is the easy part. The hard part is the hand-off: a hospital asks for everything, so patients share the whole file or nothing. MedVault shares by visit, by item and for a set time, and logs every view.

The share switch

Live

One control decides what the front desk sees. Try the three states.

On until you stop

Inside the share

Every share is view-only and has an end time. Downloads stay off, and the patient sees each time the desk opens the profile.

Every report, one vault.

How it flows

Five screens, one line through a hospital visit.

  1. 01Home
  2. 02Vault
  3. 03Share for a visit
  4. 04Medicines
  5. 05Access

The visit, start to finish

  1. Before

    Fill it once

    Set up a profile and scan old papers into the vault.

  2. Request

    The desk asks

    The front desk asks for your details for tomorrow's visit.

  3. Consent

    You choose what goes

    Approve item by item, and the form fills at the desk.

  4. After

    The prescription comes home

    It lands in the vault, with reminders and refills.

Try the flow

Drag the slider or tap the screen.

HomeShareVaultScanRefill

On the desk, too

Consent has two sides. The front desk gets a prefilled form, sees what was shared and what stayed locked, and knows when access ends.

Reflections

  1. Storage was the brief. Sharing was the problem.Every app we studied could hold a PDF; none let the patient decide who sees it.
  2. Ask what they'll share, not what they have.Item-by-item consent turned a privacy worry into one screen of switches.
  3. Design the desk too.A prefilled form only helps if the hospital trusts it. That is what I would test next, with front-desk staff.
Story · Along a battery's life

Battery Aadhaar · in research

Every EV battery has a past.

Almost nobody can see it.

How healthy is this pack? Is it safe for a second life? Where does it go after?

One ID per pack.

India's draft Battery Pack Aadhaar would give every pack its own identity.

Health, cell by cell.

First life, second life, recycling.

The service lives in the handovers between them.
